title: Turkey-Israel Rivalry Turns Military in Syria as Israel Strikes Air Base to Block Turkish Deployment; Ankara Seeks Netanyahu's Arrest via Interpol
subhead: Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria to pre-empt what it called an imminent Turkish troop deployment, pushing the two US allies' rivalry from rhetoric toward direct military friction. Ankara responded by seeking Netanyahu's arrest through Interpol, while Washington's envoy called the strike an 'unnecessary escalation.'

sections.heading: Turkey-Israel Rivalry Turns Military in Syria
sections.body:
Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria last week, with Israeli officials saying the strike was intended to prevent what they described as the imminent deployment of Turkish forces there. Turkey and Syria both denied any such deployment was planned, and no one was killed in the strike, according to the New York Times and News18.

The exchange has escalated sharply. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has called Israel a 'terror state' and compared Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to Hitler, while Netanyahu has described Erdogan as an 'antisemitic dictator,' per News18. Two days after the strike, Turkey announced it would seek Netanyahu's arrest through Interpol over charges including genocide and torture in a domestic case linked to Israel's treatment of pro-Palestine activists intercepted at sea en route to Gaza.

US Ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack called the Israeli action an 'unnecessary escalation' and urged both governments to prioritise dialogue, while US officials have since worked to restore communication between Ankara and Jerusalem.
sections.whyItMatters: Two US allies with warm ties to the Trump administration are now competing militarily inside Syria, where Israel has occupied southern territory since Assad's fall and Turkey backs President Ahmed al-Sharaa. The strike shows their rivalry can move from diplomatic confrontation to military action quickly, even if direct war remains unlikely.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Process Moves to Implementation
sections.body:
The PKK peace process is shifting from declarations to implementation. A Monitoring and Evaluation Board chaired by Vice-President Cevdet Yilmaz held its first meeting on August 24, bringing together Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, and set up four working groups on legal issues, disarmament, monitoring and social reintegration, per The Hindu.

A law passed by Parliament on August 10 — approved by 468 of 592 lawmakers — provides conditional amnesty for PKK-linked offences including membership, assisting the organisation, propaganda and financing terrorism. Prison sentences can be suspended and investigations put on hold for five to 10 years, with cases dropped if no terrorism-related offences occur in that period. Those convicted of intentional killings are excluded, as are those serving life without parole for pre-2005 offences — which means Abdullah Ocalan himself would not benefit. The PKK has called the law a 'beginning' but cited 'serious shortcomings' and continues to demand Ocalan's release.
sections.whyItMatters: The process is now institutionalised with a government oversight structure and a legal framework, moving beyond the failed attempts of 2015. But the exclusion of Ocalan and the PKK's conditional response leave the hardest political questions unresolved.

sections.heading: EU Rapporteur Calls Turkey 'Authoritarian' as Imamoglu Trial Intensifies
sections.body:
European Parliament's permanent rapporteur for Turkey, Nacho Sanchez Amor, used a visit to Istanbul to observe the trial of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu to deliver blunt criticism. 'You cannot both disrespect the court decisions and claim that your judiciary is independent. You are authoritarian. You cannot pretend to be a democrat,' he said in an interview with Turkish journalist Sirin Payzin, per Syrian Press.

Sanchez Amor said the case against Imamoglu — involving 140 alleged crimes — was political, that testimony had failed to substantiate key allegations, and that authorities had moved to ban a book Imamoglu intended to publish before its release. He contrasted that speed with the prolonged proceedings in the case of philanthropist Osman Kavala, whose release the European Court of Human Rights ordered in a ruling Ankara has not implemented.
sections.whyItMatters: The rapporteur's language is unusually direct and lands as Ankara weighs its relationship with Europe's rights system — a question Ankara itself floated this week after the Strasbourg Kavala ruling. The Imamoglu trial is the live test of whether Turkey's judiciary acts independently, and it is now central to the stalled EU accession debate.

sections.heading: Turkish and Somali Forces Free Hijacked Vessel in Deadly Operation
sections.body:
Turkish and Somali forces freed the MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged Turkish vessel hijacked on August 17 off the coast of Somalia, Somalia's defence ministry said Saturday, per AP. The operation destroyed four pirate boats and killed 14 alleged pirates; the remaining pirates fled, allowing forces to take control of the ship.

The operation was conducted under the defence cooperation agreement between Somalia and Turkey, aimed at strengthening maritime security and combating piracy. The hijacking had raised fresh concerns about a resurgence of piracy along Somalia's coast, a problem amplified by the wider disruption to shipping from the US-Iran war.
sections.whyItMatters: The rescue is a concrete demonstration of Turkey's deepening military footprint in the Horn of Africa, where it also has a naval presence and is drilling for oil off Somalia. It also puts Turkey's capabilities directly against the piracy surge that has followed the Gulf conflict's disruption of maritime routes.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact Eyes Expansion as Bangladesh and Iran Signal Interest
sections.body:
The Mecca Pact — the mutual defence agreement Turkey signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan this month — is drawing new members. Bangladesh has signalled interest in joining, while Iran and Egypt are also reported as possible members, according to News24 and The Daily Asian Age. India is closely monitoring Dhaka's signals, with analysts noting the pact has strengthened Pakistan's hand in West Asia.

Analysts cited by News18 said the agreement was partly intended to create a counterweight to Israeli influence in the region, and Turkey's participation in the bloc is now a factor in its broader rivalry with Israel across the Middle East, Horn of Africa and Eastern Mediterranean.
sections.whyItMatters: If Bangladesh joins, the pact would extend a Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan security axis into South Asia, complicating India's neighbourhood calculus. Iran's possible entry would be a geopolitical shock, potentially aligning Tehran with a bloc that includes its regional rivals.

sections.heading: Syria-Turkey Trade Grows as Ankara and Damascus Target $10 Billion
sections.body:
Syria and Turkey are seeking to increase bilateral trade from about $3.7 billion to $10 billion, according to Enab Baladi, even as economists warn that Syrian local industry faces pressure from the opening of the border. The trade push comes as Turkey deepens its political and military support for President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government in Damascus.

The economic relationship is intertwined with the security one: Turkey's backing of al-Sharaa is a central driver of the friction with Israel, which has destroyed much of Syria's military equipment since Assad's ouster and occupied territory in the south.
sections.whyItMatters: A near-tripling of bilateral trade would bind Damascus's reconstruction to Ankara's economy, cementing Turkey's position as Syria's primary external patron — and deepening the strategic stakes of the Turkey-Israel standoff over Syria.

bottomLine: The defining development of the day is the militarisation of the Turkey-Israel rivalry inside Syria: Israel's strike on Abu al-Duhur to block a feared Turkish deployment, Ankara's Interpol arrest request for Netanyahu, and Washington's public rebuke of the strike all point to a competition that has moved from rhetoric to direct military friction. Meanwhile, the Kurdish peace process is institutionalising with a working oversight board and conditional amnesty law, Turkey demonstrated its Horn of Africa reach by freeing a hijacked vessel off Somalia, and the Mecca Pact is drawing interest from Bangladesh and possibly Iran. The EU's rapporteur sharpened his 'authoritarian' verdict on Turkey as the Imamoglu trial intensifies. The central question going forward is whether Washington can manage two allies whose ambitions now collide on the ground in Syria.
sources: New York Times, News18, AP News, The Hindu, Syrian Press, Enab Baladi, News24, The Daily Asian Age, Moneycontrol, Anadolu Agency (via anews.com.tr)
